title: Workplace coaching in English with a psychologist, online – Blooming
description: One-to-one workplace coaching with a psychologist with over ten years in HR: working in Italian, a new manager, a reorganisation, leading a team for the first time. Online. Free 30-minute first meeting.

data.title: Coaching for the job you already have, in a country that's still new to you.

p.t: You have a job, and something about it isn't working: the meetings in Italian, perhaps, or a manager whose expectations you can't read. Workplace coaching with a psychologist who has worked in HR for over ten years is one-to-one work on your current job, online, in English. A hard week at work tends to follow you home, so the sessions also look at how it's affecting the rest of your life.

data.title: Work can get harder in ways nobody warned you about.

items.title: You work in Italian all day, and it costs you more than anyone sees

p.t: You follow most of the meeting, but by the time you've built the sentence, the discussion has moved on. Colleagues may think you have less to say than you do. Your Italian is improving; what you need is a way to take part that doesn't leave you drained by Wednesday.

items.title: Your manager or your team works in a way you weren't prepared for

p.t: Decisions seem to get made somewhere you aren't, and feedback arrives in a form you don't know how to read. The gap is real, and it can turn into friction with one person that slowly takes up all your attention.

items.title: A reorganisation has changed your job around you

p.t: A merger, a new manager or a role rewritten without much discussion. You're still doing your work, but you're no longer sure what's expected of you or where you stand.

items.title: You're leading a team for the first time

p.t: Perhaps you were promoted from within, or hired to manage people who have worked together for years, possibly in a language that isn't your first. Delegating feels new, and so does giving feedback to people who used to be your peers.

items.title: You're stuck, and the motivation has gone

p.t: You do what's needed and not much more, and you've stopped expecting anything to change. Before deciding anything big, you'd like to understand what's happened and what could shift.

data.title: Coaching starts from your situation, then one or two goals you choose.

p.t: Workplace coaching is focused, practical work on your current job and your next steps there, in one-to-one video sessions. It's led by a registered psychologist, and it isn't therapy: the attention stays on what you want to change at work and how.

items.title: The first sessions: your situation, then your goals

p.t: Your psychologist asks about your role and what a good week at work would look like. She also asks about what surrounds the job, such as how much Italian you use and how settled you feel, because that shapes what's realistic. Together you choose one or two goals you'll recognise when you reach them, for example speaking up in the weekly meeting, or handing over work you've been holding on to.

items.note: Assessment tools or questionnaires, if any: to confirm with Elsa.

items.title: Then work chosen for your situation

p.t: What you do in the sessions depends on the goal. You might rehearse a difficult conversation before you have it, or prepare how to make your point in a meeting held in Italian. You might map where your time and energy go in a typical week, to see what's eating into the hours you need for your main work. If you're new to leading a team, you can plan your first one-to-ones or work out how to give feedback people can act on. When the difficulty is a manager or a team that works differently from what you know, you look at what they seem to expect and how you'd like to respond.

items.title: Between sessions, you try something at work

p.t: Each session ends with one or two things to try. The next one starts with how they went, so the work stays tied to your real job.

items.title: A regular check on progress

p.t: Every few sessions you and your psychologist look back at the goals: what has moved, what hasn't, and whether they still make sense. Coaching ends when you've reached your goals.

items.note: Or when you decide to stop: to confirm with Elsa. Written summary at the end: to confirm with Elsa.

with colleagues, your manager and the people you manage.

when you keep circling the same problem without moving.
understanding why the interest has gone, and what might bring it back.
leading people for the first time, or leading a team that's changing.
the skills and relationships that would help you move up in your current organisation. If the question is which direction to take, that's career guidance.

data.title: When the question changes, or someone else can help.

p.t: If the question becomes whether to stay in this job or look for another, that's career guidance, with the same psychologist.
Career coaching & guidance

items.term: When it's heavier than a work problem.

p.t: Sometimes what looks like stress at work turns out to need something coaching isn't designed for: anxiety that doesn't switch off at the weekend, low mood that lasts, sleep that has gone. Your psychologist will tell you and can suggest working with one of our psychotherapists. With your consent, the two of them can talk to each other.

p.t: Questions about your contract, your rights at work or a formal dispute need the relevant professional, such as an employment lawyer. Coaching can help you prepare for a difficult conversation, but it isn't legal advice.

data.title: A psychologist who is also an HR professional.

people.name: Workplace coaching

p.t: Workplace coaching is led by a psychologist, registered with the Italian Order of Psychologists since 2014, whose entry in the register states that she offers sessions in English. In more than ten years in HR, she has worked on recruitment, development, training, organisation and change management, which is much of the ground workplace coaching covers. She knows the Italian job market. As a psychologist, she can also notice when the strain of a job is affecting more than the job, and say so.
